legend: A neuroblastoma from a patient with a known germline pathogenic MAX variant. This tumour is morphologically indistinguishable from a sporadic neoplasm.

MAX immunohistochemistry for the tumour in Fig. <<28217>>. The non-neoplastic inflammatory cells and endothelial cells demonstrate preserved positive staining for MAX, whereas there is loss of staining in the neoplastic cells of the neuroblastoma. Although some authors have found that MAX immunohistochemistry could have a role in triaging patients for genetic testing for MAX germline mutation, others have found that it lacks sensitivity and specificity, and it is not recommended in routine clinical practice.
An example from a patient with a known germline pathogenic MAX variant. This tumour is morphologically indistinguishable from a sporadic neoplasm.

MAX immunohistochemistry in a section of the tumour in Fig. <<28219>>. The non-neoplastic inflammatory cells demonstrate preserved positive staining for MAX, whereas there is decreased expression in the neoplastic cells of the phaeochromocytoma component as well as in the Schwannian spindle cells and ganglion cells of the ganglioneuroma component. This tumour is morphologically indistinguishable from a sporadic neoplasm.
An example from a patient with a known germline pathogenic MAX variant. This tumour is morphologically indistinguishable from a sporadic neoplasm.

MAX immunohistochemistry in a section of the tumour in Fig. <<28221>>. The non-neoplastic inflammatory cells demonstrate preserved positive staining for MAX, whereas there is variable loss of staining in the ganglion cells and Schwannian stromal cells of the ganglioneuroma. The variable loss of expression in this case illustrates the difficulty in interpreting MAX immunohistochemistry in routine clinical practice.
An example from a patient with acromegaly and a known pathogenic germline MAX variant. This tumour is morphologically indistinguishable from a sporadic neoplasm.

GHRH immunohistochemistry of the tumour in Fig. <<28576>> from a patient with secondary acromegaly due to GHRH-producing MAX-related paraganglioma and/or phaeochromocytoma. The tumour cells are positive for GHRH, whereas the stromal cells are negative.
